blocks.p: Raphael goes on to tell how Michael and Gabriel were sent out to battle against Satan and his angels. The first fight is described. Satan and his powers withdraw under cover of night. He calls a council and invents devilish engines, which in the second day’s fight throw Michael and his angels into some disorder; but at length they pull up mountains and overwhelm both the forces and the machines of Satan. Yet since the tumult does not end even so, God on the third day sends the Messiah, his Son, for whom he had reserved the glory of that victory. The Son comes to the place in the power of his Father, makes all his legions stand still on either side, and, driving with his chariot and thunder into the midst of his enemies, pursues them, unable to resist, toward the wall of Heaven. The wall opens, and they leap down in horror and confusion into the place of punishment prepared for them in the Deep. The Messiah returns in triumph to his Father.

v: “All night the fearless angel, unpursued,
Through Heaven’s wide plains kept on his way, till Morn,
Roused by the circling Hours, with rosy hand
Unbarred the gates of light. There is a cave
Within the Mount of God, close by his throne,
Where light and darkness in perpetual round
Lodge and dislodge by turns, which makes through Heaven
Welcome succession, as of day and night:
Light issues forth, and at the other door
Compliant darkness enters, till her hour
To veil the heavens, though darkness there might well
Seem twilight here. And now went forth the Morn
Such as in highest Heaven, arrayed in gold
Empyreal; from before her vanished Night,
Shot through with eastern beams; when all the plain,
Covered with thick embattled squadrons bright,
Chariots and flaming arms, and fiery steeds
Reflecting blaze on blaze, first met his view.
War he perceived, war in array, and found
Already known what he as news had thought
To have reported. Gladly then he mixed
Among those friendly powers, who welcomed him
With joy and acclamations loud, that one,
Out of so many myriads fallen, yet one
Returned not lost. On to the sacred hill
They led him, loudly cheered, and brought him up
Before the throne supreme; from which a voice
Out of a golden cloud was mildly heard:
“’Servant of God, well done; well have you fought
The better fight, who single have maintained
Against revolted multitudes the cause
Of truth, in words more potent than their arms;
And for the testimony of truth have borne
Universal reproach, far worse to bear
Than violence: for this was all your care,
To stand approved in sight of God, though worlds
Judged you perverse. The easier conquest now
Remains to you, helped by this host of friends,
Back on your foes more glorious to return
Than, scorned, you went away, and to subdue
By force those who refuse to take for law
Right reason as their law, and for their king
Messiah, who by right of merit reigns.
Go, Michael, prince of all the hosts of Heaven,
And you, in military prowess next,
Gabriel: lead forth to battle these my sons
Invincible, lead forth my armed saints
By thousands and by millions ranged for fight,
Equal in number to that godless crew
Rebellious; them with fire and hostile arms
Fearlessly charge, and to the brow of Heaven
Pursuing, drive them out from God and bliss
Into their place of punishment, the gulf
Of Tartarus, which, ready, opens wide
Its fiery Chaos to receive their fall.’
“So spoke the sovereign voice, and clouds began
To darken all the hill, and smoke to roll
In dusky wreaths with struggling flames, the sign
Of wrath aroused; nor with less dread the loud
Ethereal trumpet sounded from on high;
At which command the powers militant
That stood for Heaven, in mighty square conjoined
Of union irresistible, moved on
In silence their bright legions, to the sound
Of instrumental harmony that breathed
Heroic ardor to adventurous deeds
Under their godlike leaders, in the cause
Of God and his Messiah. On they move,
Indissolubly firm; no hill ahead,
Nor narrowing vale, nor wood, nor stream divides
Their perfect ranks; for high above the ground
Their march was, and the yielding air upbore
Their nimble tread: as when the entire race
Of birds in orderly array on wing
Came, summoned over Eden, to receive
Their names from you; so over many a tract
Of Heaven they marched, and many a province wide,
Ten times the length of this our earth. At last,
Far on the horizon to the north appeared
From edge to edge a fiery region, stretched
In battle aspect, and on nearer view
Bristling with upright shafts innumerable
Of rigid spears, and helmets thronged, and shields
Various, with boastful emblems there portrayed:
The banded powers of Satan hurrying on
With furious expedition; for they thought
That very day, by fighting or surprise,
To win the Mount of God, and on his throne
To set the envier of his state, the proud
Aspirer; but their thoughts proved foolish, vain,
Midway. And strange it seemed to us at first
That angel should with angel go to war,
And meet in fierce array, who used to meet
So often at the feasts of joy and love,
Unanimous, as sons of one great Sire,
Hymning the eternal Father. But the shout
Of battle now began, and rushing sound
Of onset ended soon each milder thought.
“High in the midst, exalted like a god,
The Apostate in his sun-bright chariot sat,
Idol of majesty divine, enclosed
With flaming cherubim and golden shields;
Then stepped down from his gorgeous throne, for now
Between the hosts but narrow space was left,
A dreadful interval, and front to front
They stood displayed in terrible array
Of hideous length. Before the cloudy van,
On the rough edge of battle not yet joined,
Satan with vast and haughty strides advanced,
Came towering, armed in adamant and gold.
Abdiel could not bear that sight, where he stood
Among the mightiest, bent on highest deeds,
And thus explores his own undaunted heart:
“’O Heaven! that such resemblance of the Highest
Should still remain where faith and honesty
Remain not! Why then should not strength and might
There fail where virtue fails, or weakest prove
Where boldest, though to sight unconquerable?
His power, trusting in the Almighty’s aid,
I mean to try, whose reason I have tried
Unsound and false; nor is it less than just
That he who in debate of truth has won
Should win in arms, in both disputes alike
Victor; though brutish that contest and foul,
When reason has to deal with force, yet so
Most reason is that reason overcome.’
“So pondering, and from his armed peers
Stepping out opposite, halfway he met
His daring foe, enraged the more at being
Forestalled, and thus defied him, confident:
“’Proud one, we meet? Your hope was to have reached
The height of your aspiring unopposed,
The throne of God unguarded, and his side
Abandoned at the terror of your power
Or potent tongue. Fool, not to think how vain
Against the Omnipotent to rise in arms;
Who out of smallest things could without end
Have raised incessant armies to defeat
Your folly; or with solitary hand,
Reaching beyond all limit, at one blow,
Unaided, could have finished you, and whelmed
Your legions under darkness. But you see
All are not of your train; there are who choose
Faith and devotion to their God, though then
To you not visible, when I alone
Seemed in your world mistaken to dissent
From all: my sect you see; now learn too late
How few sometimes may know, when thousands err.’
“The grand Foe, with a scornful sidelong eye,
Thus answered: ‘Ill for you, but in the hour
Of my revenge, you, first sought out, return
From flight, seditious angel, to receive
Your merited reward, the first assault
Of this right hand provoked, since first that tongue,
Inspired with contradiction, dared oppose
A third part of the gods, in synod met
Their deities to assert, who, while they feel
Vigor divine within them, can allow
Omnipotence to none. But well you come
Before your fellows, ambitious to win
From me some plume, that your success may show
Destruction to the rest. This pause between
(Lest you should boast unanswered) lets you know:
At first I thought that liberty and Heaven
To heavenly souls had been all one; but now
I see that most through sloth would rather serve,
Ministering spirits, trained in feast and song.
Such you have armed, the minstrelsy of Heaven,
Servility with freedom to contend,
As both their deeds compared this day shall prove.’
“To whom in brief thus Abdiel stern replied:
‘Apostate, still you err, and find no end
Of erring, from the path of truth remote.
Unjustly you defame it with the name
Of servitude, to serve whom God ordains,
Or nature: God and nature bid the same,
When he who rules is worthiest, and excels
Those whom he governs. This is servitude:
To serve the unwise, or him who has rebelled
Against his worthier, as yours now serve you,
Yourself not free, but to yourself enslaved;
Yet basely dare deride our ministry.
Reign in your kingdom, Hell; and let me serve
In Heaven God ever blessed, and his divine
Commands obey, the worthiest to be obeyed;
Yet chains in Hell, not realms, expect. Meanwhile,
From me returned, as once you said, from flight,
This greeting on your impious crest receive.’
“So saying, a noble stroke he lifted high,
Which hung not, but so swift with tempest fell
On the proud crest of Satan that no sight,
Nor motion of swift thought, much less his shield,
Could stop such ruin. Ten huge paces back
He reeled; the tenth, on bended knee, he braced
Upon his massive spear; as if on earth
Winds underground, or waters forcing way
Sidelong, had pushed a mountain from its seat,
Half sunk, with all its pines. Amazement seized
The rebel Thrones, but greater rage, to see
Their mightiest thus foiled; joy filled ours, and shouts,
Presage of victory, and fierce desire
Of battle; at which Michael bade them sound
The archangel trumpet. Through the vast of Heaven
It sounded, and the faithful armies rang
Hosanna to the Highest. Nor stood at gaze
The adverse legions, nor less hideous joined
The horrid shock. Now storming fury rose,
And clamor such as never until now
Was heard in Heaven; arms clashing on armor brayed
Horrible discord, and the maddening wheels
Of brazen chariots raged; dire was the noise
Of conflict; overhead the dismal hiss
Of fiery darts in flaming volleys flew,
And, flying, vaulted either host with fire.
So underneath that fiery vault there rushed
The two main hosts, with ruinous assault
And inextinguishable rage; all Heaven
Resounded, and had earth been then, all earth
Would to its center shake. What wonder, when
Millions of fierce encountering angels fought
On either side, the least of whom could wield
These elements, and arm himself with force
Of all their regions? How much more of power
Army against army numberless to raise
Dreadful combustion, warring, and disturb,
Though not destroy, their happy native seat,
Had not the eternal King omnipotent
From his stronghold of Heaven high overruled
And limited their might; though numbered such
As each divided legion might have seemed
A numerous host, in strength each armed hand
A legion; led in fight, yet leader seemed
Each warrior singly, as in chief; expert
When to advance, or stand, or turn the sway
Of battle, when to open, when to close
The ridges of grim war. No thought of flight,
None of retreat, no unbecoming deed
That argued fear; each on himself relied,
As if in his arm only the moment lay
Of victory. Deeds of eternal fame
Were done, but infinite: for wide was spread
That war, and various; sometimes on firm ground
A standing fight; then, soaring on main wing,
Tormented all the air; all air seemed then
Conflicting fire. Long time in even scale
The battle hung; till Satan, who that day
Prodigious power had shown, and met in arms
No equal, ranging through the dire attack
Of fighting seraphim confused, at length
Saw where the sword of Michael smote, and felled
Squadrons at once; with huge two-handed sway
Brandished aloft, the horrid edge came down,
Wide-wasting. Such destruction to withstand
He hastened, and opposed the rocky orb
Of tenfold adamant, his ample shield,
A vast circumference. At his approach
The great archangel from his warlike toil
Desisted, glad, as hoping here to end
This civil war in Heaven, the Archfoe subdued
Or captive dragged in chains; with hostile frown
And visage all inflamed, first thus began:
“’Author of evil, unknown till your revolt,
Unnamed in Heaven, now plentiful, as you see,
These acts of hateful strife, hateful to all,
Though heaviest by just measure on yourself
And your adherents: how have you disturbed
Heaven’s blessed peace, and into nature brought
Misery, uncreated till the crime
Of your rebellion! How have you instilled
Your malice into thousands, once upright
And faithful, now proved false! But think not here
To trouble holy rest; Heaven casts you out
From all her confines. Heaven, the seat of bliss,
Allows no works of violence and war.
Away, then, and let evil go with you,
Your offspring, to the place of evil, Hell,
You and your wicked crew; there stir your broils,
Before this sword of vengeance starts your doom,
Or some more sudden vengeance, winged from God,
Hurls you down headlong with augmented pain.’
“So spoke the prince of angels; to whom thus
The Adversary: ‘Do not think with wind
Of airy threats to awe one whom with deeds
You cannot. Have you turned the least of these
To flight, or, if to fall, but that they rose
Unvanquished, that you think to deal with me
More easily, and, imperious, hope with threats
To chase me off? Do not suppose so ends
The strife which you call evil, and we name
The strife of glory; which we mean to win,
Or turn this Heaven itself into the Hell
You fable, and at least to dwell here free,
If not to reign. Meanwhile, your utmost force,
And add him called Almighty to your aid,
I do not flee, but sought you far and near.’
“They ended parley, and both braced for fight
Unspeakable; for who, though with the tongue
Of angels, can relate, or to what things
Conspicuous on earth compare, that may lift
Human imagination to such height
Of godlike power? For likest gods they seemed,
Stood they or moved, in stature, motion, arms,
Fit to decide the empire of great Heaven.
Now waved their fiery swords, and in the air
Made horrid circles; two broad suns, their shields
Blazed opposite, while expectation stood
In horror. From each side with speed withdrew,
Where thickest fight had been, the angelic throng,
And left wide field, unsafe within the wind
Of such commotion: such as, to set forth
Great things by small, if, nature’s concord broken,
Among the constellations war had sprung,
Two planets, rushing from malign aspect
Of fiercest opposition in mid sky,
Should combat, and their jarring spheres confound.
Together both, with next to almighty arm
Uplifted, threatening, one stroke they aimed
That might decide at once, and need no more,
As if no power were left; nor odds appeared
In might or swift prevention. But the sword
Of Michael from the armory of God
Was given him tempered so that neither keen
Nor solid might resist that edge: it met
The sword of Satan, with steep force to smite
Descending, cut it clean in half, nor stopped,
But with swift backward wheel, deep entering, sheared
All his right side. Then Satan first knew pain,
And writhed and twisted to and fro; so sore
The cutting sword with a dividing wound
Passed through him. But the ethereal substance closed,
Not long divisible; and from the gash
A stream of nectarous humor issuing flowed,
Sanguine, such as celestial spirits may bleed,
And stained his armor, until then so bright.
At once from every side there ran to aid him
Angels many and strong, who interposed
Defense, while others bore him on their shields
Back to his chariot, where it stood withdrawn
Far from the lines of war; they laid him there
Gnashing for anguish and despite and shame
To find himself not matchless, and his pride
Humbled by such rebuke, so far beneath
His confidence to equal God in power.
Yet soon he healed; for spirits that live throughout,
Vital in every part, not as frail man
In entrails, heart or head, liver or kidneys,
Cannot but by annihilation die;
Nor in their liquid texture mortal wound
Receive, no more than can the fluid air:
All heart they live, all head, all eye, all ear,
All intellect, all sense; and as they please
They limb themselves, and color, shape, or size
Assume, whichever suits them, dense or thin.
“Meanwhile in other parts like deeds deserved
Remembrance, where the might of Gabriel fought,
And with fierce ensigns pierced the deep array
Of Moloch, furious king, who challenged him,
And at his chariot wheels to drag him bound
Threatened, nor from the Holy One of Heaven
Restrained his blasphemous tongue; but soon, cleft down
Clean to the waist, with shattered arms, in strange
And unknown pain fled bellowing. On each wing
Uriel and Raphael, each his boastful foe,
Though huge, and armed in a rock of diamond,
Vanquished, Adramelech and Asmadai,
Two potent Thrones, that to be less than gods
Disdained, but humbler thoughts learned in their flight,
Mangled with ghastly wounds through plate and mail.
Nor did Abdiel fail to wound and harry
The atheist crew, but with redoubled blow
Ariel and Arioch, and the violence
Of Ramiel, scorched and blasted, overthrew.
I might relate of thousands, and their names
Eternize here on earth; but those elect
Angels, contented with their fame in Heaven,
Seek not the praise of men. The other sort,
In might though wondrous and in acts of war,
Nor less in thirst for fame, yet by decree
Cancelled from Heaven and sacred memory,
Nameless in dark oblivion let them dwell.
For strength from truth divided and from just,
Unworthy praise, earns nothing but reproach
And ignominy, yet to glory aspires,
Vainglorious, and through infamy seeks fame:
Let then eternal silence be their doom.
“And now, their mightiest quelled, the battle swerved,
And, gored with many an inroad, shapeless rout
Entered, and foul disorder; all the ground
With shivered armor strewn, and on a heap
Chariot and charioteer lay overturned,
And fiery foaming steeds; what stood recoiled,
Exhausted, through the faint Satanic host,
Scarce holding off, or by pale fear surprised,
Then first with fear surprised and sense of pain,
Fled ignominious, to such evil brought
By sin of disobedience, till that hour
Not liable to fear or flight or pain.
Far otherwise the inviolable saints
In cubic phalanx firm advanced entire,
Invulnerable, impenetrably armed:
Such high advantages their innocence
Gave them above their foes, not to have sinned,
Not to have disobeyed; in fight they stood
Unwearied, and not subject to be pained
By wound, though from their place by violence moved.
“Now Night her course began, and over Heaven
Bringing on darkness, welcome truce imposed,
And silence on the odious din of war:
Under her cloudy cover both retired,
Victor and vanquished. On the battlefield
Michael and his victorious angels camped,
And posted round their watches as a guard,
Cherubic waving fires. On the other part
Satan and his rebellious crew had gone,
Withdrawn far in the dark, and, void of rest,
His potentates to council called by night,
And in the midst thus undismayed began:
“’O now in danger tried, now known in arms
Not to be overpowered, companions dear,
Found worthy not of liberty alone,
Too mean a claim, but what we more desire,
Honor, dominion, glory, and renown;
Who have sustained one day in doubtful fight
(And if one day, why not eternal days?)
What Heaven’s Lord had most powerful to send
Against us from around his throne, and judged
Sufficient to subdue us to his will,
But proves not so: then fallible, it seems,
In future we may deem him, though till now
Believed omniscient. True, less firmly armed,
Some disadvantage we endured, and pain,
Till now not known, but known, as soon despised;
Since now we find this our empyreal form
Incapable of mortal injury,
Imperishable, and, though pierced with wound,
Soon closing, and by native vigor healed.
Of evil, then, so small, as easy think
The remedy: perhaps more potent arms,
Weapons more violent, when next we meet,
May better us, and leave our foes the worse,
Or equal what between us made the odds,
In nature none. If other hidden cause
Left them superior, while we can preserve
Unhurt our minds, and understanding sound,
Due search and consultation will disclose.’
“He sat; and in the assembly next stood up
Nisroch, of Principalities the prime;
As one he stood escaped from cruel fight,
Sore toiled, his riven arms to havoc hewn,
And, clouded in his look, thus answering spoke:
“’Deliverer from new lords, leader to free
Enjoyment of our right as gods: yet hard
For gods, and too unequal work we find,
Against unequal arms to fight in pain,
Against the unpained, impassive; from which evil
Ruin must surely follow; for what avails
Valor or strength, though matchless, quelled with pain,
Which all subdues, and makes the hands grow slack
Of mightiest? Sense of pleasure we may well
Spare out of life, perhaps, and not complain,
But live content, which is the calmest life;
But pain is perfect misery, the worst
Of evils, and, excessive, overturns
All patience. He who therefore can invent
With what more forcible we may offend
Our yet unwounded enemies, or arm
Ourselves with like defense, to me deserves
No less than what we owe for our release.’
“To whom, with look composed, Satan replied:
“’Not uninvented, that which you aright
Believe so vital to our success, I bring.
Which of us, who beholds the bright surface
Of this ethereal mold on which we stand,
This continent of spacious Heaven, adorned
With plant, fruit, flower ambrosial, gems and gold,
Whose eye so superficially surveys
These things as not to mind from where they grow
Deep underground, materials dark and crude,
Of spirituous and fiery foam, till touched
With Heaven’s ray, and tempered, they shoot forth
So lovely, opening to the ambient light?
These, in their dark nativity, the Deep
Shall yield us, pregnant with infernal flame;
Which, into hollow engines long and round
Thick-rammed, at the other bore with touch of fire
Dilated and infuriate, shall send forth
From far, with thundering noise, among our foes
Such implements of mischief as shall dash
To pieces, and overwhelm whatever stands
Adverse, that they shall fear we have disarmed
The Thunderer of his only dreaded bolt.
Nor long shall be our labor; before dawn
Effect shall end our wish. Meanwhile revive;
Abandon fear; to strength and counsel joined
Think nothing hard, much less to be despaired.’
“He ended, and his words their drooping mood
Brightened, and their exhausted hope revived.
The invention all admired, and each, how he
To be the inventor missed; so easy it seemed,
Once found, which yet unfound most would have thought
Impossible. Yet perhaps of your race,
In future days, if malice should abound,
Someone intent on mischief, or inspired
With devilish machination, might devise
Like instrument to plague the sons of men
For sin, on war and mutual slaughter bent.
At once from council to the work they flew;
None stood to argue; innumerable hands
Were ready; in a moment up they turned
Wide the celestial soil, and saw beneath
The originals of nature in their crude
Conception; sulfurous and nitrous foam
They found, they mingled, and with subtle art,
Refined and roasted dry, they ground it down
To blackest grain, and into store conveyed.
Part dug up hidden veins (nor has this earth
Entrails unlike) of mineral and stone,
From which to found their engines and their balls
Of missile ruin; part the kindling reed
Provide, pernicious with one touch to fire.
So all before the dawn, under conscious Night,
They finished secretly, and set in order,
With silent circumspection, unespied.
“Now when fair Morn appeared in eastern Heaven,
Up rose the victor angels, and to arms
The morning trumpet sang. In arms they stood,
In golden panoply, a shining host,
Soon formed; while others from the dawning hills
Looked round, and scouts, light-armed, scour every coast,
Each quarter, to descry the distant foe,
Where lodged, or where he fled, or if for fight,
In motion or at halt. And soon they found him
Under spread ensigns, moving near, in slow
But firm battalion. Back with speediest sail
Zophiel, of cherubim the swiftest wing,
Came flying, and in midair loudly cried:
“’Arm, warriors, arm for fight! The foe at hand,
Whom we thought fled, will save us long pursuit
This day; fear not his flight: so thick a cloud
He comes, and settled in his face I see
Grim resolution, confident. Let each
His adamantine coat gird well, and each
Fit tight his helmet, grip his rounded shield,
Borne even or high; for this day will pour down,
If I guess anything, no drizzling shower,
But rattling storm of arrows barbed with fire.’
“So he warned them, aware themselves; and soon
In order, freed of all impediment,
At once, without confusion, took alarm,
And onward moved embattled; when, behold,
Not distant far, with heavy pace, the foe
Approaching, gross and huge, in hollow cube
Drawing his devilish engines, hemmed about
On every side with shadowing squadrons deep,
To hide the fraud. Both, face to face, stood still
A while; but suddenly at the head appeared
Satan, and thus was heard commanding loud:
“’Vanguard, to right and left the front unfold,
That all may see who hate us how we seek
Peace and composure, and with open breast
Stand ready to receive them, if they like
Our overture, and turn not back perverse.
But that I doubt; however, witness Heaven,
Heaven, be our witness soon, while we discharge
Freely our part. You who appointed stand,
Do as you have in charge, and briefly touch
What we propound, and loud, that all may hear.’
“So, scoffing in ambiguous words, he scarce
Had ended, when to right and left the front
Divided, and to either flank withdrew;
Which to our eyes laid bare, both new and strange,
A triple-mounted row of pillars laid
On wheels (for most like pillars they appeared,
Or hollowed bodies made of oak or fir,
With branches lopped, in wood or mountain felled),
Brass, iron, stony mold, had not their mouths
With hideous orifice gaped on us wide,
Portending hollow truce. At each, behind,
A seraph stood, and in his hand a reed
Stood waving, tipped with fire; while we, perplexed,
Stood gathered in, absorbed in our own thoughts,
Not long; for sudden, all at once, their reeds
Put forth, and to a narrow vent applied
With delicate touch. At once, in one great flame,
But soon obscured with smoke, all Heaven appeared,
From those deep-throated engines belched, whose roar
Filled the air’s bowels with outrageous noise,
And tore through all her entrails, vomiting foul
Their devilish glut, chained thunderbolts and hail
Of iron globes, which, on the victor host
Leveled, with such impetuous fury struck
That whom they hit, none on their feet could stand,
Though standing else as rocks, but down they fell
By thousands, angel on archangel rolled,
The sooner for their arms; unarmed they might
Have easily, as spirits, evaded, swift
By quick contraction or remove; but now
Foul dissipation followed and forced rout;
Nor did it help to loosen their close files.
What should they do? If on they rushed, repulse
Repeated, and indecent overthrow
Doubled, would render them still more despised,
And to their foes a laughingstock; for in view
Stood ranked of seraphim another row,
In posture to explode their second round
Of thunder; back, defeated, to return
They more abhorred. Satan beheld their plight,
And to his mates in mockery thus called:
“’Friends, why do these proud victors not advance?
A while ago they came on fierce; and when we,
To entertain them fair with open front
And breast (what more could we do?), offered terms
Of settlement, at once they changed their minds,
Flew off, and into strange vagaries fell,
As if they’d dance; yet for a dance they seemed
Somewhat extravagant and wild; perhaps
For joy of offered peace. But I suppose,
If our proposals once again were heard,
We should compel them to a quick result.’
“To whom thus Belial, in like playful mood:
‘Leader, the terms we sent were terms of weight,
Of hard content, and full of force, urged home,
Such as we might perceive amused them all,
And stumbled many; who receives them right
Had need from head to foot well understand;
Not understood, this gift they have besides:
They show us when our foes can’t walk upright.’
“So they among themselves in jesting vein
Stood scoffing, heightened in their thoughts beyond
All doubt of victory; eternal might
To match with their inventions they presumed
So easy, and of his thunder made a scorn,
And all his host derided, while they stood
Awhile in trouble. But they stood not long;
Rage prompted them at length, and found them arms
Against such hellish mischief fit to oppose.
At once (behold the excellence, the power
Which God has in his mighty angels placed!)
Their arms away they threw, and to the hills
(For earth has this variety from Heaven,
Of pleasure, laid out over hill and dale)
Light as the lightning’s glimpse they ran, they flew;
From their foundations, loosening to and fro,
They plucked the seated hills with all their load,
Rocks, waters, woods, and by the shaggy tops
Uplifting bore them in their hands. Amazement,
Be sure, and terror seized the rebel host,
When, coming at them, dreadful, they beheld
The bottoms of the mountains upward turned;
Till on those cursed engines’ triple row
They saw them whelmed, and all their confidence
Under the weight of mountains buried deep;
Themselves invaded next, and on their heads
Main promontories flung, which in the air
Came shadowing, and bore down whole legions armed;
Their armor helped their harm, crushed in and bruised
Into their substance pent, which wrought them pain
Implacable, and many a dolorous groan,
Long struggling underneath, before they could wind
Out of such prison, though spirits of purest light,
Purest at first, now gross by sinning grown.
The rest, in imitation, to like arms
Betook themselves, and tore up neighboring hills;
So hills amid the air encountered hills,
Hurled to and fro in dreadful volleying,
That underground they fought in dismal shade:
Infernal noise! War seemed a civil game
To this uproar; horrid confusion heaped
Upon confusion rose. And now all Heaven
Had gone to wreck, with ruin overspread,
Had not the almighty Father, where he sits
Shrined in his sanctuary of Heaven secure,
Consulting on the sum of things, foreseen
This tumult, and permitted all, by design,
That his great purpose he might so fulfill,
To honor his anointed Son, avenged
Upon his enemies, and to declare
All power on him transferred: so to his Son,
Who sits beside him on his throne, he spoke:
“’Effulgence of my glory, Son beloved,
Son in whose face the invisible is seen
Made visible, what by Deity I am,
And in whose hand what by decree I do,
Second Omnipotence: two days are past,
Two days, as we compute the days of Heaven,
Since Michael and his powers went forth to tame
These disobedient. Fierce has been their fight,
As likeliest was, when two such foes met armed;
For to themselves I left them; and you know
Equal in their creation they were formed,
Save what sin has impaired, which yet has wrought
Insensibly, for I suspend their doom;
So in perpetual fight they must go on
Endlessly, and no solution can be found.
War, wearied, has performed what war can do,
And to disordered rage let loose the reins,
With mountains as with weapons armed, which makes
Wild work in Heaven, and dangerous to the whole.
Two days are therefore past; the third is yours.
For you I have ordained it, and thus far
Have suffered, that the glory may be yours
Of ending this great war, since none but you
Can end it. Into you such virtue and grace
Immense I have transfused, that all may know
In Heaven and Hell your power beyond compare,
And this perverse commotion governed thus,
To manifest you worthiest to be heir
Of all things, to be heir and to be king
By sacred unction, as your rightful due.
Go, then, you mightiest, in your Father’s might;
Ascend my chariot, guide the rapid wheels
That shake Heaven’s basis; bring forth all my war,
My bow and thunder; my almighty arms
Gird on, and sword upon your potent thigh;
Pursue these sons of darkness, drive them out
From all Heaven’s bounds into the utter Deep:
There let them learn, as suits them, to despise
God and Messiah, his anointed King.’
“He said, and on his Son with rays direct
Shone full; he all his Father full expressed
Ineffably into his face received;
And thus the filial Godhead, answering, spoke:
“’O Father, O supreme of heavenly Thrones,
First, highest, holiest, best, you always seek
To glorify your Son, I always you,
As is most just; this I my glory count,
My exaltation, and my whole delight,
That you, in me well pleased, declare your will
Fulfilled, which to fulfill is all my bliss.
Scepter and power, your giving, I assume,
And gladlier shall resign, when in the end
You shall be all in all, and I in you
Forever, and in me all whom you love.
But whom you hate, I hate, and can put on
Your terrors, as I put your mildness on,
Image of you in all things; and shall soon,
Armed with your might, rid Heaven of these rebels,
To their prepared ill dwelling driven down,
To chains of darkness and the undying worm,
Who from your just obedience dared revolt,
Whom to obey is happiness entire.
Then shall your saints, unmixed, and from the impure
Far separate, circling your holy mount,
Unfeigned hallelujahs to you sing,
Hymns of high praise, and I among them chief.’
“So saying, bowing on his scepter, he rose
From the right hand of Glory where he sat;
And the third sacred morn began to shine,
Dawning through Heaven. Forth rushed with whirlwind sound
The chariot of paternal Deity,
Flashing thick flames, wheel within wheel, undrawn,
Itself instinct with spirit, but convoyed
By four cherubic shapes; four faces each
Had wondrous; as with stars, their bodies all
And wings were set with eyes; with eyes the wheels
Of beryl, and careering fires between;
Over their heads a crystal firmament,
On which a sapphire throne, inlaid with pure
Amber, and colors of the showery arch.
He, in celestial panoply all armed
Of radiant Urim, work divinely wrought,
Ascended; at his right hand Victory
Sat eagle-winged; beside him hung his bow
And quiver with three-bolted thunder stored;
And from about him fierce effusion rolled
Of smoke and flickering flame and sparks of dread.
Attended by ten thousand thousand saints,
He onward came; far off his coming shone;
And twenty thousand (I their number heard)
Chariots of God, half on each hand, were seen.
He on the wings of cherub rode sublime
On the crystalline sky, in sapphire throned,
Illustrious far and wide, but by his own
First seen: unlooked-for joy surprised them all
When the great ensign of Messiah blazed
Aloft, by angels borne, his sign in Heaven;
Under whose leading Michael soon drew back
His army, spread out wide on either wing,
Under their Head embodied all in one.
Before him power divine prepared his way;
At his command the uprooted hills withdrew
Each to its place; they heard his voice and went
Obedient; Heaven its wonted face renewed,
And with fresh blossoms hill and valley smiled.
“His hapless foes saw this, but stood obdurate,
And to rebellious fight rallied their powers,
Insensate, hope conceiving from despair.
In heavenly spirits could such perverseness dwell?
But to convince the proud what signs avail,
Or wonders move the obdurate to relent?
They hardened more by what might most reclaim,
Grieving to see his glory; at that view
Took envy, and, aspiring to his height,
Stood re-embattled fierce, by force or fraud
Hoping to prosper, and at length prevail
Against God and Messiah, or to fall
In universal ruin last; and now
To final battle drew, disdaining flight
Or faint retreat; when the great Son of God
To all his host on either hand thus spoke:
“’Stand still in bright array, you saints; here stand,
You angels armed; this day from battle rest.
Faithful has been your warfare, and by God
Accepted, fearless in his righteous cause;
And as you have received, so have you done,
Invincibly. But of this cursed crew
The punishment to other hand belongs;
Vengeance is his, or one he solely names.
Number to this day’s work is not ordained,
Nor multitude; stand only and behold
God’s indignation on these godless poured
By me. Not you but me they have despised,
Yet envied; against me is all their rage,
Because the Father, to whom in Heaven supreme
Kingdom and power and glory all belong,
Has honored me according to his will.
Therefore to me their doom he has assigned,
That they may have their wish, to try with me
In battle which the stronger proves: they all,
Or I alone against them; since by strength
They measure all, of other excellence
Not emulous, nor care who may excel them;
Nor other strife with them will I allow.’
“So spoke the Son, and into terror changed
His countenance, too severe to be beheld,
And full of wrath bent on his enemies.
At once the Four spread out their starry wings
With dreadful shade contiguous, and the orbs
Of his fierce chariot rolled, as with the sound
Of torrent floods, or of a numerous host.
He on his impious foes right onward drove,
Gloomy as night; under his burning wheels
The steadfast empyrean shook throughout,
All but the throne itself of God. Full soon
Among them he arrived, in his right hand
Grasping ten thousand thunders, which he sent
Before him, such as in their souls infixed
Plagues. They, astonished, all resistance lost,
All courage; down their idle weapons dropped;
Over shields and helms, and helmed heads he rode
Of Thrones and mighty seraphim prostrate,
That wished the mountains now might be again
Thrown on them as a shelter from his ire.
Nor less on either side tempestuous fell
His arrows, from the fourfold-visaged Four,
Distinct with eyes, and from the living wheels,
Distinct alike with multitude of eyes;
One spirit in them ruled, and every eye
Glared lightning, and shot forth pernicious fire
Among the accursed, that withered all their strength,
And of their wonted vigor left them drained,
Exhausted, spiritless, afflicted, fallen.
Yet half his strength he never used, but checked
His thunder in mid-volley; for he meant
Not to destroy, but root them out of Heaven.
The overthrown he raised, and as a herd
Of goats or timorous flock together thronged
Drove them before him thunderstruck, pursued
With terrors and with furies to the bounds
And crystal wall of Heaven; which, opening wide,
Rolled inward, and a spacious gap disclosed
Into the wasteful Deep. The monstrous sight
Struck them with horror backward, but far worse
Urged them behind: headlong themselves they threw
Down from the verge of Heaven; eternal wrath
Burned after them to the bottomless pit.
“Hell heard the unbearable noise; Hell saw
Heaven ruining from Heaven, and would have fled
Affrighted; but strict Fate had cast too deep
Her dark foundations, and too fast had bound.
Nine days they fell; confounded Chaos roared,
And felt tenfold confusion in their fall
Through his wild anarchy, so huge a rout
Encumbered him with ruin. Hell at last,
Yawning, received them whole, and on them closed;
Hell, their fit habitation, fraught with fire
Unquenchable, the house of woe and pain.
Disburdened Heaven rejoiced, and soon repaired
The breach within her wall, rolled back in place.
Sole victor from the expulsion of his foes,
Messiah turned his triumphal chariot.
To meet him all his saints, who silent stood
Eyewitnesses of his almighty acts,
With jubilee advanced; and as they went,
Shaded with branching palm, each order bright
Sang triumph, and they sang him conquering King,
Son, Heir, and Lord, to him dominion given,
Worthiest to reign. He, celebrated, rode
Triumphant through mid-Heaven, into the courts
And temple of his mighty Father, throned
On high; who into glory him received,
Where now he sits at the right hand of bliss.
“Thus measuring things in Heaven by things on earth,
At your request, and that you may beware
By what is past, to you I have revealed
What might have else from humankind been hid:
The discord that befell, and war in Heaven
Among the angelic powers, and the deep fall
Of those too high aspiring, who rebelled
With Satan, he who envies now your state,
Who now is plotting how he may seduce
You also from obedience, that with him,
Bereaved of happiness, you may partake
His punishment, eternal misery;
Which would be all his solace and revenge,
As a despite done against the Most High,
To win you once companion of his woe.
But do not listen to his temptings; warn
Your weaker; let it profit you to have heard
By terrible example the reward
Of disobedience. Firm they might have stood,
Yet fell; remember, and fear to transgress.”

blocks.p: the circling Hours (3). The Horae, goddesses of the seasons, who in Homer keep the gates of heaven.
There is a cave (4). Heaven has its own gentle alternation of light and shade, which our day and night only imitate.
Servant of God, well done (29). Echoes the master’s praise in the parable of the talents and Paul’s “good fight” [Matt. 25:21; 1 Tim. 6:12].
Right reason (42). In Renaissance thought, the God-given power by which the mind perceives the moral law.
Tartarus (54). In Greek myth the deepest pit of the underworld, where the rebel Titans were chained; here, Hell.
in mighty square (62). Milton’s “quadrate,” the square battle formation of ancient armies.
Their names from you (76). Raphael’s aside to Adam, who named the birds and beasts [Gen. 2:19–20].
to the north (79). The north was Satan’s quarter, where he set up his rebel throne [Isa. 14:13].
adamant (110). A legendary substance of unbreakable hardness.
my sect (147). Abdiel takes up the scornful word for a small dissenting faction and wears it with pride.
A third part of the gods (156). A third of the angels fell with Satan [Rev. 12:4].
Hosanna (205). Hebrew “save, we pray,” a shout of praise [Ps. 118:25; Matt. 21:9].
malign aspect / Of fiercest opposition (313–314). In astrology, planets directly opposite each other in the sky were thought to exert their most hostile influence.
nectarous humor … sanguine (332–333). Angels bleed not blood but a fluid like nectar, the drink of the gods; “sanguine” means blood-red.
They limb themselves (352). Spirits give themselves limbs, and any shape, at will, as Book I also says of the fallen angels.
Adramelech and Asmadai (365). Adrammelech, an Assyrian idol to whom children were burned, and Asmodeus, the evil spirit of the book of Tobit [2 Kings 17:31; Tob. 3:8].
Ariel, Arioch, Ramiel (371–372). Rebel names drawn from Hebrew and apocryphal sources; “Ariel” means “lion of God.”
cubic phalanx (399). A solid square formation; the cube was an emblem of firmness and perfection.
Nisroch (447). An Assyrian god, in whose temple Sennacherib was murdered [2 Kings 19:37]. Principalities are a rank of angels.
implements of mischief (488). Satan’s invention is the cannon; Ariosto and Spenser had likewise made gunpowder the devil’s work.
sulfurous and nitrous foam (512). Sulfur and saltpeter, which with charcoal make gunpowder.
conscious Night (521). Night as a knowing witness to their secret work.
Zophiel (535). A cherub’s name meaning “spy of God.”

terms of weight … walk upright (621–627). Belial’s puns, extending Satan’s mock “overture” (562): the “terms” are cannon shot, “understand” plays on standing up under the blows, and “stumbled” means both puzzled and tripped.
Effulgence of my glory (680). The Son as the radiance of the Father’s glory, the visible image of the invisible God [Heb. 1:3; Col. 1:15].
Second Omnipotence (684). The Son, acting with the Father’s full power.
sacred unction (709). Anointing; “Messiah” means “anointed one” [Ps. 2:2, 6–8].
sword upon your potent thigh (714). From the psalm of the warrior king [Ps. 45:3].
all in all (732). At the end the Son will hand the kingdom back to the Father [1 Cor. 15:24–28].
chains of darkness and the undying worm (739). Scripture’s images of the punishment of the fallen [2 Pet. 2:4; Mark 9:44].

The chariot of paternal Deity (750–759). Drawn from Ezekiel’s vision: four living creatures with four faces, wheels within wheels full of eyes, a crystal firmament, and a sapphire throne ringed with a rainbow, the “showery arch” [Ezek. 1:4–28; 10:9–14].
beryl (756). A precious stone, sea-green or golden.
Urim (761). Gems on the high priest’s breastplate, used to learn God’s will [Exod. 28:30].
ten thousand thousand … twenty thousand (767–770). The numbers of God’s hosts given in Scripture [Dan. 7:10; Ps. 68:17].
Vengeance is his (808). “Vengeance is mine,” says the Lord [Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19].
wished the mountains (842–843). As the wicked will call on the mountains to fall on them [Rev. 6:16].
Distinct with eyes (846). Studded or adorned with eyes.
Nine days they fell (871). As the Titans in Hesiod fell nine days from heaven; compare the nine days on the burning lake in Book I.
Your weaker (909). Eve, called the “weaker vessel” [1 Pet. 3:7].
